claims.text: Thermal aging above a critical temperature promotes Mg segregation from the metastable solid solution.
Thermally activated diffusion is the process responsible for local Mg segregation.
Local Mg segregation facilitates nucleation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Thermal aging causes the nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds from a metastable HEA solid solution.
The thermally formed intermetallic compounds are specifically Mg-rich.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds disrupt the continuity of the homogeneous protective solid-solution matrix.
Disruption of the solid-solution matrix impairs formation of passivating oxide layers.
Second-phase or intermetallic development can reduce corrosion resistance.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds increases high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
Samples aged above the critical temperature will contain newly formed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates detectable by in situ XRD and TEM.
Samples aged above the critical temperature will have a statistically significant increase in corrosion rate relative to as-processed samples.
Samples aged above the critical temperature will have statistically significantly faster oxidation kinetics relative to as-processed samples.
Aging below the critical transformation temperature preserves the metastable protective state.
Exposure above the critical transformation temperature triggers intermetallic formation and loss of corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The as-processed alloy has a homogeneous metastable solid solution with high corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
